implementation_notes: Mockito builds the test-specific subclass at runtime: spy(sut) (or @Spy) is a proxy whose unstubbed methods call the real implementation, and doReturn(...).when(sut).now() replaces only the boundary; thenCallRealMethod() does the same for a plain mock. Because the proxy is generated, self-calls inside the real code are the trap to know: with the subclass mock maker they dispatch to the real object, while Mockito 5's default inline mock maker instruments the class itself and can also mock final types. The hand-written route still needs the method to be non-final and visible (protected or package-private with the test in the same package).
pitfalls: spy() copies the real instance: state mutated through the spy is not reflected in the original, and Mockito special-cases equals/hashCode.

With the subclass mock maker a self-call inside the real object cannot be intercepted (only calls arriving through the mock reference can); final types need the inline mock maker (default since Mockito 5) or a hand-written seam.
private, static and final seams cannot be overridden at all, and an anonymous test subclass cannot touch private members of the SUT.

variants.name: Hand-written test subclass (anonymous or named)
variants.implementation_notes: The literal pattern, zero dependencies: an anonymous subclass inside the test method or a named class in the test source set overrides the boundary method and exposes setters/getters for private state (protected visibility usually has to be granted in production - Meszaros's visibility note). It needs a non-final class and method, works on every JVM without runtime bytecode generation, and pairs with assertion libraries alone; writing @Override is essential because a signature typo would otherwise silently fail to override.
pitfalls: Without @Override a signature typo silently fails to override; the test then exercises the real boundary and may still pass.
A final class or method, or a private seam, blocks the subclass at compile time; protected must be granted in production, which is impossible for third-party code.
The subclass inherits the SUT's constructor side effects (I/O, caches, registration) - override only after constructing, or extract the work out of the constructor.
